core_concept.name: SCOBY OIL-SPILL SORBENT SPONGE
core_concept.intended_use: Absorb floating petroleum/oil contamination from water or contaminated surfaces using a low-density bacterial-cellulose-derived sorbent, then recover as much absorbed oil as practical before controlled recycling or disposal of the spent sorbent.

findings: Hydrophobically engineered bacterial-cellulose aerogels have demonstrated high oil/organic-solvent sorption and mechanical squeeze recovery in laboratory studies.

A 2025 superhydrophobic bacterial-cellulose aerogel reported density near 5.8 mg/cm3 and sorption across tested oils/solvents of about 80.91-203.30 g/g, retaining performance over 20 absorption-desorption cycles.
A 2024 hydrophobic bacterial-cellulose aerogel reported saturation capacities about 42.14-85.37 g/g and oil/water separation efficiency of 98.48% in its tested system.
A 2025 all-biomass carbonized aerogel from bacterial cellulose and chitin reported about 138 g/g oil absorption after controlled freeze-drying and carbonization.
bacterial_cellulose_oil_sorbents.important_boundary: These values are laboratory results for specifically engineered aerogels/composites. They must not be treated as expected performance for raw or simply air-dried SCOBY.

native_scoby_limit.finding: Native bacterial cellulose is strongly hydrophilic. High oil-over-water selectivity generally appears after pore-preserving drying and/or hydrophobic surface engineering or controlled carbonization.
native_scoby_limit.implication: A raw wet SCOBY pellicle is not the lead field sorbent architecture.

tea_feedstock_question.question: Which tea type should be used to maximize final oil uptake?

known_primary_result.study: Characterization of cellulose production by a Gluconacetobacter xylinus strain from Kombucha
known_primary_result.finding: For the strain and conditions studied, green-tea medium produced approximately 0.20 g/L cellulose versus approximately 0.14 g/L in black-tea medium.
known_primary_result.interpretation: This supports green tea as a useful production-yield arm, not as proof that green-tea-derived cellulose absorbs more oil.

screening_matrix.reason: Higher bacterial-cellulose yield than black tea in one primary strain comparison.
Common kombucha substrate and direct comparator in primary literature.
Do not prioritize until green-vs-black matched data exist.

tea_feedstock_question.decision_rule: Choose feedstock by dry cellulose yield, final aerogel density, porosity, oil uptake, water uptake, oil/water selectivity, mechanical integrity and cost; tea identity alone never decides the winner.

stage_1_coupon.purpose: Fast matched screening of feedstock and drying branches.

stage_1_strip.purpose: Same area as the square coupon but useful for bend, retrieval and layered-boom tests.

stage_3_module.boundary: These are mass-balance illustrations using published laboratory capacities, not field-performance promises. Real crude oil, waves, suspended solids, viscosity, temperature, water competition and retrieval losses can reduce performance substantially.

D0_PRESSED_AIR_DRY.expected_tradeoff: Good handling strength but likely lower sorption because capillary pore volume collapses during dense drying.

D1_AIR_DRY_LOW_COMPACTION.expected_tradeoff: More open than pressed film but still likely to shrink and densify substantially.

D2_FREEZE_DRY_UNMODIFIED.expected_tradeoff: High pore volume but native hydrophilicity may cause strong water uptake and poor selectivity.

D3_FREEZE_DRY_HYDROPHOBIC.evidence: Closest architecture to high-capacity laboratory bacterial-cellulose oil sorbents.
D3_FREEZE_DRY_HYDROPHOBIC.boundary: Surface chemistry must be selected for environmental compatibility and validated for leaching before field deployment.

D4_CONTROLLED_CARBONIZED_AEROGEL.evidence: Controlled carbonized biomass aerogels show high hydrophobicity and oil uptake in primary research.
D4_CONTROLLED_CARBONIZED_AEROGEL.boundary: Requires controlled thermal processing and atmosphere characterization; not a household process.

D5_MICROWAVE_TREATED.reason: Microwave treatment can create spatial hot spots, steam, arcing, ignition and uncontrolled thermal decomposition; visual charring or foaming does not establish useful aerogel structure or safe composition.

matched_experiment_design.sample_geometry: 50 x 50 mm coupons for the first pass
matched_experiment_design.control_rule: Use the same SCOBY consortium, sugar loading, fermentation time window, pellicle maturity definition, wash endpoint, wet mass normalization and test temperature across matched arms.
safe_screening_liquids: food-grade vegetable oil for first-pass uptake and squeeze-recovery measurements
clean water for water-uptake and selectivity measurements
matched_experiment_design.petroleum_gate: Do not move to crude oil or fuel-contaminated water until the safe-surrogate gate passes and testing can be done with appropriate environmental, fire, chemical and waste controls.

performance_metrics.buoyancy_retention: fraction of test duration during which module remains retrievable at the oil-water interface

promotion_gates.G1_OIL_UPTAKE: Median vegetable-oil uptake >= 10 g/g in the lead branch.
promotion_gates.G2_SELECTIVITY: Median oil/water uptake ratio >= 5 under the same drain protocol.
promotion_gates.G3_RETENTION: At least 80% of initially absorbed oil remains after standardized passive draining.
promotion_gates.G4_RETRIEVABILITY: At least 95% of sorbent dry-equivalent mass remains physically retrievable without fragmentation.
promotion_gates.G5_RECOVERY: Mechanical pressing recovers >= 50% of absorbed surrogate oil without catastrophic structural breakup if oil recovery is part of the product route.
promotion_gates.G6_REPLICATION: Lead result reproduced in at least two independent SCOBY batches.
promotion_gates.G7_PETROLEUM: Only after G1-G6: licensed or appropriately controlled petroleum-spill simulation with hydrocarbon analysis and waste plan.
promotion_gates.G8_FIELD: Field deployment requires ecological leachate testing, buoyancy/retrieval validation, contaminant-specific performance, regulatory review and a complete spent-sorbent recovery plan.

field_architecture.why_not_loose_fragments: Loose sorbent particles or flakes create secondary recovery and litter problems.
design_features: large retrievable modules rather than loose powder
mechanically robust outer capture mesh if needed
low dry density and positive buoyancy
known saturated mass limit for safe handling

one_time_sponge_end_of_life.user_concept: Disposable sorbent after one field use, followed by centralized recovery of the oil fraction and processing of the contaminated cellulose fraction.
one_time_sponge_end_of_life.prohibited_shortcut: Do not compost, burn openly, microwave, shred into the environment, or return petroleum-loaded sorbent to biological fermentation.

why_microwave_is_not_the_default.reason: The key performance driver is preserving a low-density pore network while controlling wettability. Freeze-drying and controlled surface engineering have direct primary-literature support. Uncontrolled microwave treatment may collapse, char, ignite or chemically alter the material without producing the desired pore architecture.
why_microwave_is_not_the_default.research_position: Keep microwave-treated SCOBY as a separate blind material-identity branch inherited from the existing SCOBY-D0 microwave research line, not as the production recipe for an oil-spill sponge.

claim_boundaries: Published engineered BC aerogel performance is not raw SCOBY performance.
Green tea may increase BC yield under some conditions but is not proven to increase oil sorption.
A microwave-charred SCOBY is not automatically an aerogel, activated carbon, safe sorbent or field-ready material.
High laboratory g/g uptake values do not guarantee crude-oil-spill field performance.
Recovered petroleum is a contaminated process stream and requires characterization and licensed handling.
